title: Malerkotla, 1872
hook: Namdharis taken prisoner after a raid were executed by cannon on the order of British officials, without trial

segments.voice: Yesterday, Namdhari, and your line was simple and firm. Did you keep your small promise? Today ends a week that ran from Lavan, through loss and found again, to two reformers. It ends hard. Day nine hundred fifty-nine.

This is a heavy day, so here is where it goes before it starts. Malerkotla is a small town in the Punjab, the seat of a princely state. Near it, Namdhari prisoners were tied to the mouths of cannon by order of a British official, and the guns were fired. There was no trial. Namdharis remember these men as shaheeds, martyrs, and they gather at Malerkotla to remember them still. Today isn't about the details of the killing. It's about how a community remembers. Today: Malerkotla.
screen: `A HEAVY DAY.` → `PRISONERS BEFORE THE CANNON.` → `NO TRIAL.` → `HOW A COMMUNITY REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: First, what led to it. Yesterday you met the Namdharis, with their white clothes and their firm refusals. Some of them were angered by the killing of cows, and a band of them attacked Malerkotla. There was fighting, and people of the town were killed as well as Namdharis. Namdhari histories say Baba Ram Singh had not sent them, and had tried to hold his followers back. Second, the response. The British official in charge of the district had the captured men brought out and executed by cannon, without a trial. A senior official approved more executions the next day. Even the British government found this too far, and the official was removed from his post. Third, a story Namdharis tell. Among the prisoners, they say, was a young boy. The official offered to spare him if he would deny his teacher. The boy refused, and was cut down. Treat this as the community's memory, told and retold, rather than a court record. Fourth, why it's remembered. The daily Ardas, the prayer Sikhs stand for, calls to mind those who gave their lives and kept their faith, and it ends by asking for the good of all, sarbat da bhala. Remembering, in that prayer, is not revenge. At Malerkotla, the town's own people were caught in the violence too, and this lesson keeps the same silence for their dead. That's the shape of today's line: saying the names, not letting them disappear, and not turning grief into a weapon.
screen: `A RAID, AND DEATHS ON BOTH SIDES.` · `EXECUTED BY CANNON, WITHOUT TRIAL.` · `A STORY NAMDHARIS TELL.` · `REMEMBERING, NOT REVENGE.` · then, large: `REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: Two minutes, and one of them in silence. For the first minute, breathe slowly and let the week settle: Lavan, a loss remembered, something found again, two reformers. Then, for one full minute, keep silence for those who died at Malerkotla, the prisoners and the townspeople alike. No words needed. If you pray, you can stay with Waheguru in the quiet. If you don't, just hold the silence as a way of saying they mattered. The bell holds the time.
Malerkotla. The town in the Punjab where captured Namdharis were executed by cannon without trial, and where they're remembered as martyrs. Today's word.
Your line: remembered. Today, say one name of someone who's gone, out loud or in your head, and let it be enough. Day nine hundred fifty-nine.
